questions.problem:
A billiard ball is projected vertically downward with an initial velocity of $0.25\,\text{m/s}$ and hits the ground after $0.025$ minutes. Find the distance the billiard ball covered during its fall. **Do not round your answer**.

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*

During its fall, the billiard ball covered a distance of
{{field-1}}$\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the billiard ball is $u=0.25\,\text{m/s}.$

- We can find the time it takes for the billiard ball to fall in seconds as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =0.025\,\text{min} \\  & =0.025\,\text{min}\cdot \frac{60\,\text{s}}{\text{min}} \\  & =0.025\,\cancel{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{60\,\text{s}}{\cancel{\text{min}}} \\  & =1.5\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\  & =(0.25)(1.5)+\frac{1}{2}(9.8)(1.5)^{2} \\  & =0.375+11.025 \\  & =11.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $11.4\,\text{m}.$

questions.problem:
A block is projected vertically downward from the top of a building under construction with an initial velocity of $1\,\text{m/s}$ and hits the ground after $10$ seconds. Find the distance the block covered during its fall.

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the block is $u=1\,\text{m/s}.$

- The block falls for $t=10\,\text{s}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\  & =(1)(10)+\frac{1}{2}(9.8)(10)^{2} \\  & =10+490 \\  & =500\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $500\,\text{m}.$

questions.problem:
An object is projected vertically down from a bridge with a height of $22\,\text{m}.$ It takes $2\,\text{s}$ to hit the water below. What was the initial velocity of the object?

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The object falls for $t=2\,\text{s}.$

- The object covers the distance of $s=22\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $u,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\ (22) & =u(2)+\frac{1}{2}(9.8)(2)^{2} \\ 22 & =2u+19.6 \\ 2.4 & =2u \\ u & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the initial velocity of the object was $u=1.2\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
A stone is projected vertically downward from a height of $29.4\,\text{m}$ with an initial velocity of $17.64\,\text{km/h}.$ How long will it take for the stone to hit the ground?

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*

The stone hits the ground in{{field-1}}seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- We can find the initial velocity of the stone in meters per second as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =17.64\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \\  & =17.64\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}\cdot \frac{1000\,\text{m}}{\text{km}}\cdot \frac{\text{h}}{60\,\text{min}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{60\,\text{s}} \\  & =17.64\,\frac{\cancel{\text{km}}}{\cancel{\text{h}}}\cdot \frac{1000\,\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{km}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{h}}}{60\,\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{60\,\text{s}} \\  & =17.64\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{m}}{{60}^{2}\,\text{s}} \\  & =4.9\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

- The stone covers the distance of $s=29.4\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(29.4) & =(4.9)t+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (9.8){t}^{2} \\ 29.4 & =4.9t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 6(4.9) & =(4.9)t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 6\cancel{(4.9)} & =\cancel{(4.9)}t+\cancel{(4.9)}{t}^{2} \\ 6 & =t+{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+t-6 & =0 \\ (t+3)(t-2) & =0 \\ t & =-3,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the stone hits the ground after $t=2$ seconds.

canonical_examples.problem: A penny is projected vertically downward with an initial velocity of $300 \, \textrm{m/min}$ and hits the ground after $2$ seconds. Find the distance the penny covered during its fall.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- We can find the initial velocity of the object in meters per second as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =300\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}} \\  & =300\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{60\,\text{s}} \\  & =300\,\frac{\text{m}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{60\,\text{s}} \\  & =\frac{300}{60}\cdot \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \\  & =5\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

- The penny falls for $t=2\,\textrm{s}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\  & =(5)(2)+\frac{1}{2}(9.8)(2)^{2} \\  & =10+19.6 \\  & =29.6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $29.6\,\textrm{m}.$

Example: 
                    Solving for Time
canonical_examples.problem: A stone is projected vertically downward from a height of $19.6\,\textrm{m}$ with a velocity of  $14.7\,\textrm{m/s}.$ How long will it take for the stone to hit the ground?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the stone is $u=14.7\,\textrm{m/s}.$

- The stone covers the distance of $s=19.6\,\textrm{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}19.6 & =(14.7)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 4(4.9) & =3(4.9)t+(4.9){t}^{2} \\ 4\cancel{(4.9)} & =3\cancel{(4.9)}t+\cancel{(4.9)}{t}^{2} \\ 4 & =3t+{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+3t-4 & =0 \\ (t+4)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =-4,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the stone hits the ground after $t=1$ second.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Imagine a ball is dropped from a $78.4\,\text{m}$ rooftop. How do we determine how long it will take for the ball to hit the ground?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266313/assets/4567e8adbdb04e413ed6b6b5fdbc8e5d6aa07f86fab8bca9f5c6980ab14c9adf.png)

We can show that the distance traveled by a falling object can be modeled using the quadratic function

$$
s=ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2.
$$

This equation looks tricky, so let's go through each variable: 

- $s$ is the **displacement** of the object, measured in meters. For our purposes, the displacement measures the object's distance from the starting point.

- $u$ is the **initial velocity** of the object, measured in meters per second.

- $t$ is time, measured in seconds.

- $g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2$ is a constant known as the **acceleration due to gravity.**  It tells us the acceleration of a falling object close to the earth's surface.

In our example, we want to find the time it takes for a ball to fall a distance of 

$$
s =78.4\,\textrm{m}.
$$

Since the ball was *dropped*, its initial velocity was zero. Therefore, we have

$$
u = 0 \,\textrm{m/s}.
$$

Substituting the known values into our equation for $s$ and solving for $t,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}78.4 & =(0)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 78.4 & =4.9{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{78.4}{4.9} \\ {t}^{2} & =16 \\ t & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have two solutions, $t=4$ and $t=-4$ seconds. However, we are only interested in the positive solution because the ball hits the ground after some positive duration of time has passed. 

Therefore, the ball will hit the ground after $t=4$ seconds.

tutorials.name: Deriving the Formula
tutorials.problem:
Let's show that the distance traveled by an object with constant acceleration can be modeled using the quadratic function

$$
s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2,
$$

where $u$ is the object's initial velocity, $t$ is time, and $a$ is the acceleration.

Plotting this situation on a velocity-time diagram, we obtain the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14266313/assets/1b8f3f4843728863d39409a52c0dafeb05baed9d20b0244d8a3dd640bca36c2d.png)

Notice that:  

- Our object has initial velocity $u.$ This corresponds to the point $(0,u)$ on the diagram.

- At time $t$ our object has velocity $v.$ This corresponds to the point $(t,v)$ on the diagram.

- The acceleration $a$ corresponds to the slope of the line connecting $(0,u)$ and $(t,v).$

Calculating the slope of the line, we have

$$
a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}
$$

which can be written as

$$
v = u + at.
$$

Next, recall that the distance $s$ covered by the object corresponds to the area below the line. Since the area under the graph is a trapezoid, the distance $s$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =\frac{({\text{base}}_{1}+{\text{base}}_{2})}{2}\cdot \text{height} \\  & =\frac{(u+v)}{2}\cdot t \\  & =\frac{u+(u+at)}{2}\cdot t \\  & =\frac{(2u+at)t}{2} \\  & =ut+\frac{1}{2}a{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

When dealing with a motion under gravity it's common to let $a=g=9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2,$ the acceleration due to gravity.

tutorials.name: Modeling Assumptions
tutorials.problem:
In this topic, we made the following assumptions:

- All objects are treated like a **particle**, a small point with no length, width, or height.

- All objects move vertically down in a straight line, so acceleration due to gravity is taken as positive.

- The only acceleration the objects have is due to gravity, and any other forces (such as wind resistance) are negligible.

steps.title: Modeling Assumptions
steps.html:
Modeling Assumptions
?

In this topic, we made the following assumptions:

  • All objects are treated like a particle, a small point with no length, width, or height.

  • All objects move vertically down in a straight line, so acceleration due to gravity is taken as positive.

  • The only acceleration the objects have is due to gravity, and any other forces (such as wind resistance) are negligible.
